FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (Part 1) (Second Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft 
finalized by the Nuclear Energy for Peaceful Applications Sectional Committee, had been approved by the 
Chemical Division Council. 


Measurement of gross beta activity is often used as a substitute for determination of individual radionuclides, 
because it is simple and rapid. But the data is of no use for interpretation. The gross beta activity is of use only 
for comparison purposes and does not fulfil the purpose of individual radionuclide analysis. In this method, the 
total beta activity of prepared samples is counted by Geiger Muller (GM) counting system. Keeping in view this 
fact, the Committee had decided to formulate this standard in 1994. The calibration of GM counter for measuring 
the total beta activity of mixed fission products is a difficult problem. The effective energy of the fission products 
changes with time and most samples have considerable mass so that self-absorption becomes an important factor. 
Normal practice is to use the radiation from natural potassium as a standard for the beta activity of mixed fission 
products. 


This standard was originally published in 1994 and later revised in 2013 due to technological advancement in 
this field and the experience gained with the time. In the first revision, modifications were made in use of low- 
background gas flow GM Counter for accurate result, sample size, standard background count and efficiency, 
source of standard potassium, time for count, and in calculations to account the uncertainties associated with the 
counting. 

In this revision, modifications have been made with respect to detection system in use of low-background beta 
counting system, preparation of sample for water with high dissolved solids and in calculations. Terminology, 
which are common with other parts of IS 14194 have been modified and made uniform among all the parts of the 
standard. 

All laboratories shall be duly certified by Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Govt of India for carrying out analysis 
or measurement of radioactivity in commodities. 


This Indian Standard is being published in five parts. The other parts of this standard are: 
Part 2 Gross alpha activity 
Part 3 Uranium 
Part 4 Radium 
Part 5 Sampling 
The list of experts who contributed significantly to the formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 


In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical 
values ( revised )’. 


IS 14194 (Part 1) : 2020 


Indian Standard 


RADIONUCLIDES IN ENVIRONMENTAL SAMPLES — 
METHODS OF ESTIMATION 
PART 1 GROSS BETA ACTIVITY MEASUREMENT 


(Second Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard (Part 1) prescribes the method of 
measurement of gross-beta activity applied to water, 
waste water, soil, smears, gummed paper, air filters, 
ash of vegetation and biological samples and other 
materials to estimate contamination from industrial 
exposure, fallout and natural background. 


2 REFERENCES 


The standards listed below contain provisions which, 
through reference in this text, constitute provisions of 
this standard. At the time of publication, the editions 
indicated were valid. All standards are subject to 
revisions, and parties to agreements based on this 
standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility 
of applying the most recent editions of the standards 
listed below: 


IS No. Title 
264 :2005 Nitric acid (third revision) 
265:1993 Hydrochloric acid (fourth revision) 
1070: 1992 Reagent grade water — Specification 
(third revision) 
3 TERMINOLOGY 


For the purpose of this standard the following 
terms shall apply. 


3.1 Activity — The number of spontaneous nuclear 
transformations occurring in a given quantity of 
material during a suitably small interval of time divided 
by that interval of time. It is commonly expressed in 
Becquerel (Bq), formerly expressed in Curies. 


NOTE — Sometimes used to designate a quantity of 
radionuclide (also called disintegration rate). 


3.2 Nuclide — A species of atom characterized by its 
mass number, atomic number and nuclear energy state, 
provided that the mean life in that state is long enough 
life time usually more than 10" s to be observable. 


3.3 Radionuclide — An unstable form of a chemical 
element that radioactively decays, resulting in the 
emission of nuclear radiation. 


4 PRINCIPLE 


For measurement of beta activity of water, waste water, 
soil, gummed paper, air filters, ash of vegetation and 
biological samples, the samples taken are prepared 
with suitable treatment (digestion) and then measured 
for beta activity by a low background beta counter. 


5 EQUIPMENT 


5.1 Low Background Beta Counter — Low back- 
ground beta counter of background less than 0.05 cps 
with about 30 percent efficiency for potassium-40 betas. 
The system shall be sensitive and capable to detect 
gross B activity below 0.2 mBq/m’? and 30 mBd/L, for 
air and for drinking water samples respectively. 


5.2 Shielding to Detector — Sufficient shielding to 
reduce the counting system background to 0.05 cps or 
less (generally, about 50.8 mm lead shield is in use). 


5.3 Sample Holder Assembly — Capable of taking 
planchets of minimum 25 mm diameter with 2 to 3 mm 
rims. 


5.4 Aluminium or Stainless Steel Planchet — Of 
minimum 25 mm diameter and with 2 to 3 mm rims. 


5.5 Air Oven 
5.6 Infrared Lamp — Of maximum 500 W. 
5.7 Muffle Furnace 


6 PREPARATION OF SAMPLE 


For the gross activity estimation, preparation of sample 
should be simple and fast. The methods of sampling 
prescribed in 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4 and 6.5 are usually 
followed for the environmental samples to be tested 
for radioactivity of water, soil, vegetation, biological 
samples, air filters, gummed paper or filter paper swipe 
samples. All the samples collected, shall be properly 
labelled, giving the following details: 


a) Sample no; 

b) Description of samples; 

c) Location of sample collection; and 
d) Date of collection. 


IS 14194 (Part 1) : 2020 


6.1 Water with Low Dissolved Solids (< 100 mg/l) 


6.1.1 Total dissolved solid in water sample is measured 
with TDS meter. 


6.1.2 Collect the water sample in a pre-cleaned 
polythene bottle after rinsing with same water. 300 
to 500 ml of the sample should be sufficient for gross 
activity determination. To preserve the samples, use 
hydrochloric acid (HCl) (see IS 265) or nitric acid 
(HNO,) (see IS 264) to obtain a pH < 2 at the time of 
sample collection. 


6.1.3 Take a sample of 300 ml in a clean glass beaker 
and evaporate on a hot plate near dryness to about 5 ml. 
Avoid baking solid on evaporation container. 


Transfer 1 ml of this water to the aluminium planchet 
kept under infrared lamp. Put on the lamp and evaporate 
to dryness. Repeat this process to transfer all 5 ml 
samples after rinsing with distilled water (see IS 1070). 
Dry the sample under infrared lamp completely. 


6.1.4 Cool the completely dried sample planchet. Add 
2 drops of 1 percent collodion in acetone. Allow the 
acetone to evaporate. This sample should be counted in 
the beta counter. 


6.2 Water with High Dissolved Solids (= 100 mg/l) 


6.2.1 Take 500 ml from the 1 000 ml of water sample. 
Add 2 mi concentrated hydrochloric acid, stir and 
then add 5 mg ferric chloride or ferric nitrate as iron 
carrier, 2mg of calcium nitrate or calcium chloride as 
Ca-carrier. Warm on a hot plate and add 25 ml 
sulkowitch reagent (see Note) and 8 N ammonia with 
stirring until precipitate forms. 


Add 5 mg of ammonium molybdenum phosphate 
(AMP) and stir it using a magnetic stirrer for about 
1 h till complete precipitation take place or alternatively 
stir it well with a glass rod and keep it overnight to 
settle the precipitate. 

NOTE — Sulkowitch reagent is 2.5 g of oxalic acid, 2.5 g of 


ammonium oxalate, 5ml of acetic acid and distilled water to 
make 150 ml. 


6.2.2 Separate ferric hydroxide by decanting and 
centrifuging. Wash the precipitate with 10 ml distilled 
water twice and discard washings. 


6.2.3 Slurry the ferric hydroxide precipitates with 1 ml 
distilled water and transfer to a 25 mm aluminium 
planchet using a glass dropper with attached rubber 
teat. Dry the slurry under an infra red lamp and transfer 
the precipitate completely using further small amount 
of distilled water. 


6.2.4 Dry the planchet under infrared lamp. Ferric 
hydroxide when dried, flakes off (use a pointed glass 
rod to spread the sample uniformly in the planchet). 


After cooling the planchet, add a drop or two of 
1 percent collodion in acetone and dry. The planchet is 
ready for counting. 


6.3 Soil 


6.3.1 Take the surface soil (up to a depth of 5 cm) 
from the required location. Sample can be taken from 
a known area using a square or rectangular frame 
of known area, when activity has to be expressed as 
Bq/m?. Homogenize the soil sample using quadrating 
or coning method and then take representative sample. 
Remove pebbles and grass root in that portion, dry the 
sample in an oven at 110°C. Destroy organic matter in 
a muffle furnace below 300°C. Powder the soil using a 
mortar and pestle. 


6.3.2 Take 25 mg of dry soil powder in a 25 mm 
diameter aluminium planchet. Spread evenly, add a 
few drops of 1 percent collodion solution to fix it to the 
planchet and then count in beta counter. 


NOTE — Sample thickness should be below 5.0 mg/cm? 


6.4 Vegetation/Soft Tissues of Biological Samples 


6.4.1 Take known weight (100 g) of the sample, dry it 
in oven at 110°C. Take the dry weight and powder the 
dry material in a grinder. 


6.4.2 Take 25 mg of the powdered sample in the 
aluminium planchet and fix it with a few drops of 
1 percent collodion solution. Count the sample in a 
beta counter. 


6.4.3 If the sample does not give any detectable count, 
ash a known weight of dried sample in a muffle furnace 
at 300°C. 


6.4.4 Take the ash weight and grind the ash to fine 
powder. 


6.4.5 Mount 25 mg of ash powder on an aluminium 
planchet and count in a beta counter after fixing it with 
a few drops of 1 percent collodion solution. 


6.5 Air Filters or Gummed Paper Deposits or Filter 
Paper Swipes 


6.5.1 Ifthe sampling is done on a filter paper disc fixed 
on 25 mm air sampling head, it can be mounted directly 
to an aluminium planchet and count for beta activity. 


6.5.2 Ifthe sampling filters disc is of bigger diameter or 
rectangular ofknown area as in the case ofhigh volume 
samplers, cut 24 mm diameter discs from the sample 
and mount on an aluminium planchet and count for beta 
activity. 


6.5.3 In the case of air sampling the set up should have 
a flowmeter and a time totalizer (manual timer) to 
estimate the volume of air filtered. 


NOTE — Record the flow rate at the beginning and the ending 
of the sample and take the average of these two for calculating 
the volume of air sampled. 


6.5.4 In case of swipe sample, note the area over which 
the swipe sample taken. Swipe samples are taken to 
estimate loose contamination on any surface. 


6.5.5 In case of gummed paper deposition collection 
for evaluating the dry fallout deposition, the area 
of collection paper should be known for evaluating 
Bq/m’ deposition. 


7 CALIBRATION 


7.1 For calibration, the normal practice is to use the 
radiation from potassium chloride of minimum purity 
level 99 percent (100 mg in an aluminium planchet) as a 
standard for the beta activity of mixed fission products. 
The average energy of potassium-40 is 0.40 MeV 
(E... = 1.31 MeV). This is the best approximation of the 
energy for mixed fission products among the available 
long-lived isotopes. Alternatively electroplated 
Chlorine-36 beta sources with average energy of 
0.24 MeV and E =0.71MeV can be used. 


max 
NOTE —The potassium activity is taken from the nuclear data 
sheets of the National Academy of Sciences. The values are 
28 betas per second per gram of potassium, and 3.5 gamma 
photons/s/g of potassium. 


7.2 The mass of the actual samples can usually be 
approximated quite well by a suitable mass of potassium 
chloride. In some cases where a more active standard is 
desired, pressed pellets are made up with several grams 
of potassium chloride (with a few percent of sodium 
stearate). These standards are first calibrated against the 
proper weight of potassium chloride and then are used 
merely to check reproducibility of the counters. 


8 ACTIVITY MEASUREMENTS 


8.1 Keep the low background beta counter ‘ON’ for 
at least an hour to stabilize in case the counter is not 
already ‘ON’. 


8.2. Take 3 600 s background counts with a blank 
aluminium planchet. 


IS 14194 (Part 1) : 2020 


8.3 Determine the efficiency of the counter using a 
standard potassium-40 source (100 mg KCl). 


8.4 Keep the sample planchet in the counting system 
and count for 3 600 s.

connected matters in the country.

Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 
“BIS Catalogue” and “Standards: Monthly Additions’.
